title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We present artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a concise nearest‑work comparison, and precise preregistered protocol modifications required to obtain a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, no transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two contrasting architectural approaches are common in recent research and engineering practice. Translation‑first architectures constrain the generation space via a vendor‑aware DSL, apply formal verification, and rely on solver/repair only when constraints are violated; these approaches prioritize deterministic device guarantees. Agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines centralize generation in a single LLM and rely on deterministic validators and bounded repair/rollback to achieve correctness while preserving generator flexibility.

This study's preregistered head‑to‑head question was: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation: reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), and analysis by the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Critically, the preregistered execution semantics used shared_initial_candidate: each pair received one identical LLM candidate (one model call shared between arms). That semantic removes generator variance by design and therefore makes the run a measurement of downstream deterministic validator acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than a direct test of independent generator or repair robustness. The present paper reports the frozen preregistration, exact execution accounting, all principal numeric outcomes (contingency counts, bootstrap parameters, repair flags), an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping required by peer review, and concrete minimal protocol modifications (also preregisterable) that would enable a discriminating independent‑generator head‑to‑head comparison.
sections.related_work: Two research traditions frame our contribution. First, the formal translation→verification literature demonstrates how constrained translation plus deterministic verification yields strong device guarantees and supports what‑if analyses and incremental checks; representative foundational works include early network verification and synthesis systems that emphasize soundness and tractable analyses [10,11,12]. Second, LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps research examines flexible generation, chain‑of‑tool orchestration, and iterative repair; these studies emphasize the need for deterministic validators to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals [13,14,15]. Prior empirical work varies in which stage it stresses: generator correctness (independent sampling), repair coverage (how often repairs recover correctness), or validator behavior (accept/reject); few studies combine preregistration, a paired design, and machine‑verifiable deterministic validation with an archived execution manifest. Our run is intentionally narrow and artifactized: it isolates validator acceptance parity under shared candidate semantics and thereby clarifies what that class of experiments can and cannot resolve relative to prior work. For immediate comparison we position three representative verified works: INTA (intent translation with LLM agents) which evaluated independent generation in ICNP 2025 [3]; a self‑correcting multi‑agent verifier pipeline for Kubernetes network policy (IFIP Networking 2026) that exercised repair loops [4]; and Weighted NetKAT / formal verification literature that emphasizes formal guarantees over generative flexibility [5]. The nearest‑work comparison matrix later summarizes axes each study covers.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary design. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) froze: the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness A − B); N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks balanced across vendor×topology clusters; model declared = gpt‑5‑mini; validator declared = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0); adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; allowed repair_iterations = 1 (repair only applied when triggered). The preregistered sampling/power rationale targeted detecting ≈15pp paired differences at ~80% power under assumptions of independent generator variance — a calculation that presumes independent generations and therefore does not apply under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and implementation. The execution contract deliberately used shared_initial_candidate: each pair used a single LLM generation performed once and provided verbatim to both pipeline arms. Practical consequences were (i) model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) while planned episodes = 240; (ii) generator variance was intentionally removed from the confirmatory estimand, which therefore measures validator acceptance parity for identical candidates. The orchestration recorded per‑call provider traces and context resets to prevent cross‑pair contamination (provider_call_audit shows cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false). The execution manifest reports: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120; these values are archived in the execution manifest.

Task generation, validator rules, and scoring. Tasks were produced by a deterministic synthetic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) that outputs intent text, initial and expected final states, required safe sequences, and canonical reference answers. The validator applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5 v5.0) that checks syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, intermediate dependency constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown→change→restore), and final state consistency; a configuration passed the end‑to‑end correctness check only if validator.validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed command counts, difficulty metadata, validation_before/after snapshots and repair_applied flags. Representative scoring JSONs are archived and linked from the manifest.

Preregistered analysis and multiplicity. Analysis followed the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor: compute paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), estimate paired difference (A − B), bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes. Secondary estimands included repair coverage and repair iteration counts; multiplicity control used Benjamini–Hochberg for subgroup tests (FDR 0.05). All analysis code, seeds, and executor configurations are archived in the analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary numeric outcomes. Execution completed all preregistered confirmatory episodes: completed_episode_count = 240 (120 paired tasks), failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (single shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced the paired contingency: n11 = 120 (both arms accepted); n10 = 0 (baseline only); n01 = 0 (guarded only); n00 = 0 (both failed). Marginal success rates: baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 (100%), guarded = 120/120 = 1.0 (100%). The primary estimand (A − B) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.0. These numeric results and bootstrap parameters are archived in analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729); the paired contingency table is recorded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv.

Repair outcomes and secondary estimands. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes; no repair iterations were executed. Consequently preregistered secondary estimands (repair coverage difference, mean repair iterations) are unobserved in this execution and provide no evidence for H2 as originally formulated. Representative per‑task traces (for example pair‑000001: execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) show shared_initial_candidate normalized_response content, validation_before.valid = true, validation_after.valid = true, and repair_applied = false.

Deterministic reconciliation and accounting checks. The deterministic reconciler confirms episode‑level accounting: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 120, baseline_success_count = 120, guarded_success_count = 120. Provider audit metadata shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and no cross_condition cache reuse. No exclusions or contamination flags were raised per the preregistered contamination checks.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: what the measured estimand is (and is not). Because the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics by design, the collected data do not measure independent generator variance, repair efficacy, or each architecture's ability to produce correct candidates when operating independently. Instead, the run robustly measures validator‑acceptance parity: for identical LLM candidates delivered to the two downstream orchestration paths, the deterministic validator accepted those candidates in both arms for all 120 pairs. The pinned bootstrap CI and McNemar p = 1.0 reflect that degenerate concordance and correctly summarize the observed data; these statistics do not support claims about independent generator superiority or repair coverage.

Evidence‑to‑claim mapping (compact). The following maps preregistered hypotheses/estimands to the measurements actually performed, the primary artifact(s) that support the assigned verdict, and the verdict.
1) H1 (Paired difference A − B > 0 for end‑to‑end correctness): Measured estimand in this execution = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics (not independent generation). Supporting artifacts: preregistration CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 (preregistration_sha256 recorded in execution manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11=120,n10=0,n01=0,n00=0). Verdict: Tested only for validator‑acceptance parity; independent generator comparison untested.
2) H2 (Agentic pipeline achieves higher repair coverage): Measured? No — repair_applied = false for all episodes. Supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied=false per episode; representative execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json), analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Verdict: Unobserved in this execution.
3) Primary estimand executed as registered: validator‑acceptance parity (A and B acceptance statuses for identical candidates). Supporting artifacts: analysis/condition_summary.csv (baseline 120/120, guarded 120/120) and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv. Verdict: Observed parity (A − B = 0.00).

Nearest‑work comparison (compact matrix). We position the present run relative to three representative verified studies along four experimental axes: independent generation sampling, repair loop instrumentation, validator acceptance focus, and emulator/hardware realism.
• INTA, ICNP 2025 [3]: emphasized intent translation with LLM agents and evaluated independent generation variance — independent generation: yes; repair loops: limited; validator acceptance: partial; emulator: yes.
• Mahmood & Song, IFIP Networking 2026 [4]: presented a self‑correcting multi‑agent pipeline with active repair/verification loops — independent generation: yes; repair loops: yes; validator acceptance: emphasized; emulator: Kubernetes policy domain.
• Weighted NetKAT / verification literature [5,10–12]: emphasized formal verification guarantees and what‑if analyses — independent generation: not applicable; repair loops: typically solver‑based; validator acceptance: core focus; emulator: verification models rather than emulation.

Operational implications and protocol recommendations. The present artifact bundle documents a reproducible protocol for validator regression testing and acceptance‑parity checks when generation is held constant; this is useful for validator benchmarking and for regression tests across orchestrators. To discriminate architectures on independent generator/repair performance, the preregistered protocol must be modified in measurable ways (all are preregisterable): (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair — model_calls_used would increase to 240 for initial candidates alone; (ii) allow multiple sampled generations per arm (capture generator variance), increasing model_calls further; (iii) enable repair iterations and instrument repair_applied counters so repair coverage > 0 can be observed and compared; (iv) increase device fidelity (hardware or higher‑fidelity emulation) to reduce simulator‑to‑hardware contamination risk. Each change has direct, manifestable consequences in the execution manifest (model_calls_used, provider_call_event counts, nonzero repair_applied flags) and therefore can be validated in future artifact archives.

Threats to validity (brief). Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate removes generator variance intentionally; hence internal conclusions are limited to validator‑acceptance parity. Construct validity: the binary deterministic acceptance metric captures syntactic/semantic correctness per validator rules but does not quantify operator‑facing explanation quality or maintainability. External validity: synthetic tasks and Mininet‑derived emulation limit production generality; single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) limit multi‑model/validator generality. Conclusion validity: degenerate concordance reduces power for detecting differences — the preregistered power calculation assumed independent generation and is not applicable here.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks the deterministic validator accepted the identical LLM candidates in both arms for all pairs (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage are therefore unobserved. The run demonstrates how preregistered shared‑candidate experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity but, by design, do not adjudicate independent generator or repair robustness. We supply artifact‑grounded evidence, a compact evidence‑to‑claim mapping, and explicit preregistered protocol modifications that would enable a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑up runs.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
